open_obligations: Note that Rahman et al.'s baseline is consultancy; check what baseline Parrish et al. used.
Check whether COVID-19 and climate-change claims count as the 'highly technical' set-up Parrish et al. mean.
Check how much the information given to the debaters drives the gain.

Note that Parrish et al.'s conclusion comes from two-turn debate in which professional writers hired through Upwork write the counter-arguments to existing arguments on QuALITY passages, whereas Rahman et al.'s debaters are two AI systems and their judges interact with two AI advisors arguing opposing sides and were recruited with either mainstream or skeptical beliefs; the debaters (human writers versus AI systems), the debate protocol and the judge population differ as well as the task.
in.other_title: AI debate helps human judges with strong prior beliefs assess controversial COVID-19 and climate claims
in.rationale: Parrish et al. conclude debate may help in other set-ups, such as highly technical tasks, though not for multiple-choice reading comprehension. Rahman et al. report that on COVID-19 and climate-change factuality claims, debate between two AI systems improves human judges' accuracy and calibration and beats consultancy by 4-10%; the comparison is with consultancy, and the claims are possibly not highly technical (see obligation 2).
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate helps human judges in set-ups other than multiple-choice reading comprehension, here contested scientific factuality claims

text: The authors conclude that debate may be helpful in other set-ups, such as highly technical tasks, but that for multiple-choice reading comprehension the debate set-up is potentially harmful to human accuracy, particularly when judges lack a strong incentive to abstain when unsure.
title: Could debate help human judges in other set-ups such as highly technical tasks?
